blocks.content: The Competition Commission of India plays a vital role in curbing anti-competitive practices and ensuring fair play across Indian markets.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Competition Commission of India (CCI) was established under the Competition Act, 2002 to enforce competition law across India.
Its core objective is to prevent practices having an appreciable adverse effect on competition (AAEC) in Indian markets.
CCI prohibits anti-competitive agreements (such as cartels) and the abuse of dominant position by market-leading enterprises.
It regulates combinations (mergers, acquisitions, and amalgamations) to ensure they do not harm healthy market competition.
The body acts as a quasi-judicial authority consisting of a Chairperson and up to six members appointed by the Central Government.

rows: Curbing concentration of economic power & monopolies
Promoting market competition and consumer welfare
Prior government approval required based on asset size
Threshold-based notification system for mergers & acquisitions

items: CCI replaced the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act, 1969 based on the recommendations of the Raghavan Committee.
Section 3 of the Competition Act addresses anti-competitive agreements, whereas Section 4 governs the abuse of dominant position.
Appeals against orders passed by the CCI are heard by the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT).
